10.6 Witness protection

10.6.1 Article 20(4) of the Constitution guarantees the right of an accused person to examine witnesses and access evidence presented against them.[footnote 133]

10.6.2 However, the Protection of Witnesses and Whistleblowers of Criminal Offences proclamation provides for the protection of witnesses, whistleblowers and certain family members. Under Article 3(1), protection measures apply in relation to testimony, information or investigations concerning offences punishable by death or by rigorous imprisonment of 10 years or more.[footnote 134]

10.6.3 The Criminal Procedure Code includes measures intended to safeguard witnesses during criminal proceedings. Article 67(c) provides that bail may be refused where an applicant is likely to interfere with witnesses or tamper with evidence.[footnote 135]

10.6.4 Article 4 of the Protection of Witnesses and Whistleblowers of Criminal Offences Proclamation sets out a range of protective measures that may be provided to witnesses, whistleblowers and other protected persons. These include physical protection, secure accommodation and relocation, concealment or change of identity, restrictions on contact by accused persons, protection of confidentiality, and the use of in camera proceedings or alternative methods of giving evidence. The proclamation also provides for financial, medical, educational and counselling assistance, compensation for harm resulting from retaliation, support for family members where a protected person dies, protection against retaliatory administrative action, and immunity from prosecution in certain circumstances where information is provided.[footnote 136]

10.6.5 Article 6 of the proclamation allows an eligible person to apply directly for protection or, where they are unable to do so, through an investigator, prosecutor or another interested person acting on their behalf.[footnote 137]

10.6.6 Various laws criminalise attacks, threats and other forms of retaliation against witnesses, whistleblowers and persons who provide information to the authorities.

Article 444(1) of the Criminal Code provides that a person who assaults, suppresses or harms an individual for giving information or evidence, or for acting as a witness in a criminal case, is punishable by 5 to 20 years’ imprisonment or a fine.[footnote 138] Article 444(2) adds that where the crime ‘has entailed grave harm to the body or health of the victim or his death, the relevant provision concerning such matters shall apply concurrently.’[footnote 139]

Article 455(2) of the Criminal Code provides that a person who, ‘by violence, intimidation or by promising or offering or giving undue advantage causes another to make false accusation or give false testimony or obstructs, through interference, the giving of testimony or the production of evidence in relation to a crime punishable with rigorous imprisonment for more than two years or obstructs law enforcement officials or public servants while exercising their official duties in relation to the same crime, is punishable with rigorous imprisonment not exceeding seven years.’[footnote 140]

Article 53 of the Anti-Corruption Special Procedure and Rules of Evidence Proclamation criminalises reprisals against whistleblowers and witnesses and requires government offices to establish procedures to protect employees from retaliation.[footnote 141]

Article 12 of the Terrorism Proclamation criminalises interference with intimidation of, inducement of, or violence against witnesses, whistleblowers and persons closely connected to them in terrorism-related cases, providing for penalties of 3 to 7 years’ rigorous imprisonment.[footnote 142]

Article 16 of the Prevention and Suppression of Terrorism Crimes Proclamation No. 1176/2020 provides that [w]here the life, wellbeing of property [sic] of any person or his family is endangered for being a witness or whistleblower of terrorist crimes, he shall be given protection in accordance with the Protection of Witnesses and Whistleblowers of Criminal Offences Proclamation No.699/2010.’ Article 16(2) provides that, without prejudice to that sub-article, ‘the court hearing the case may take the following measures: a) Change the Venue; b) Cause not to publish or record the court proceedings in part or in whole or to be released in any form.’ Contravening such an order is punishable with simple imprisonment, or, where the act ‘hinders the judicial proceedings or endangers the witness’, with ‘rigorous imprisonment from one year to seven years and with fine not exceeding Birr fifty thousands’.[footnote 143]

Article 14 of the Trafficking and Smuggling Proclamation criminalises intimidation, interference, violence, threats and other reprisals against witnesses, whistleblowers and related persons in trafficking and smuggling cases, with penalties of 3 to 7 years’ rigorous imprisonment.[footnote 144]

10.6.7 With respect to implementation of witness protection programmes the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has established a Witnesses and Whistleblowers Protection Directorate. According to information published by the MoJ, the directorate is responsible for assessing applications for protection, deciding whether protection should be granted, overseeing implementation of protection measures, and protecting witnesses and whistleblowers from threats, intimidation and reprisals linked to their testimony.[footnote 145]

10.6.8 The Ministry of Justice reported on 22 March 2025 on a study of the witness protection law conducted by its Witnesses and Whistleblowers Protection Directorate and on the resulting draft replacement proclamation. The report, in Amharic, stated (unofficial translation using AI translation tools):

‘Although Proclamation No. 699/2003 [2010] is Ethiopia’s first witness and whistleblower protection proclamation, there are various problems in its implementation and circumstances that do not allow the duty to testify to be discharged… the proclamation currently in operation to protect the safety of witnesses has fundamental legal gaps, and therefore it was necessary to prepare a proclamation that accords with current and actual conditions and meets international witness protection standards…

‘[T]he existing proclamation, by way of example, does not clearly specify to whom the power to implement the proclamation is given, does not indicate the territorial scope of application, does not specify in detail the composition of personnel — starting with the situation of the protection bodies, and the role of psychology, information technology and so on — and does not cover budget, the confidentiality of witness protection and related matters.’[footnote 146]

10.6.9 The Organised Crime Index scored Ethiopia 3.00 out of 10 on victim and witness support and noted: ‘Despite improvements, victim assistance is inconsistent, with limited services for male victims and broader organized crime cases. Witness protection measures exist, but non-state actors remain the primary service providers for victims of conflict-related sexual violence, highlighting gaps in government support.’[footnote 147]

10.6.10 The USSD TiP Report 2025 stated that the government maintained a witness protection directorate and used measures including victim support during criminal proceedings, video testimony and child-friendly interview rooms for child witnesses. However, the report also stated that protection services remained limited and that concerns about reprisals and difficulties meeting travel costs reportedly discouraged some victims from participating in criminal proceedings.[footnote 148]

10.7.1 The Advocates and WCADP April 2024 Ethiopia UPR report noted:

‘Ethiopia has not formally abolished the death penalty or implemented a moratorium on executions, nor has it limited the application of the death penalty to the “most serious” crimes. ‘As of 2023, Ethiopia has ten individuals under a death sentence. There is a de facto moratorium on the death penalty as Ethiopian authorities have not carried out any executions since 2007, but authorities have not established an official moratorium.

‘Further, Ethiopia has asserts [sic] “that the general consensus of the public at this moment is not towards abolishing the sentence of death penalty particularly for serious criminal offences.”’[footnote 149]

10.7.2 The same source added:

‘According to Article 15 of the Ethiopian Constitution, a death sentence can be carried out only when an individual has been convicted of a serious crime. Yet Ethiopia retains the death penalty for both serious and less serious crimes. For example, in 2020, authorities passed Proclamation No. 1176/2020 on the Prevention and Suppression of Terrorism Crimes, which permits the death penalty for nonviolent crimes such as “causing damage to property” that results in harm to historical sites or the natural environment.

‘According to the Criminal Code of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, a death sentence may only be passed in cases of grave crimes. In 2021, Ethiopia informed the UN Human Rights Committee that the sentencing guidelines of the Federal Supreme Court of Ethiopia were “a notable measure taken to [limit] the death penalty to only the most serious crimes.” Under Article 6, however, many offenses punishable by death do not meet the ICCPR’s definition of “serious crime,” which requires intentional killing. A death sentence may be imposed for various offenses outside of intentional murder, including: (a) habitual gang armed robbery; (b) aggravated robbery; (c) threats or acts of treason; (d) committing economic crimes during wartime; (e) espionage; and (f) failure to provide proper medical treatment that causes the death of a wounded combatant. Moreover, a provision for aggravating offenses creates the possibility for a court to impose a death sentence for crimes that otherwise do not carry the death penalty.’[footnote 150]

10.7.3 The African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR), in its concluding observations on Ethiopia’s 7th–10th periodic report following the review on 9 and 11 May 2025, stated (ACHPR July 2025 report):

10.7.4 ‘The Report indicates that capital punishment under Ethiopian law is imposed for crimes strictly considered serious and prejudicial, and that numerous procedural limitations are established to limit the execution of death sentences.

10.7.5 ‘The Delegation informed that Ethiopia has not altered its position on the abolition of the death penalty or on joining the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Nevertheless, the draft Criminal Procedure and Evidence Code includes a provision that allows a death sentence to be commuted to life imprisonment if it is not executed within two years following the judgment.

‘Currently, as of April 2025, there are 130 convicts (125 men and 5 women) on death row. All of the convicts have been found guilty and sentenced to the death penalty for exceptionally serious crimes.’[footnote 151]

10.7.6 The 2025 Amnesty International report on death sentences and executions reported more than 5 death sentences were imposed in Ethiopia during 2025 but noted that no executions were carried out. The report classified Ethiopia as a ‘retentionist’ state, indicating that the death penalty remained provided for in law.[footnote 152]

10.7.7 On 12 September 2024, Hands Off Cain, a Brussels based international NGO that advocates for the abolition of the death penalty and other forms of inhumane punishment[footnote 153] reported: ‘Ethiopia’s Defense Force announced on September 10, 2024, that it has pardoned 178 ethnic Tigrayan members of the Ethiopian Defense Force, who were sentenced to death by court martial in connection with the November 2020 attack on the Northern Command in the Tigray region of Ethiopia.’[footnote 154]

10.8 Accountability for violations committed during conflict

10.8.1 The GoE August 2024 UPR report stated that the government permitted the joint Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) and Ethiopian Human Rights Commission (EHRC) investigation into violations committed during the conflict in northern Ethiopia in 2021. According to the report, the findings and recommendations of that investigation informed the development of Ethiopia’s Transitional Justice (TJ) Policy, which was adopted on 17 April 2024 and was being implemented at the time of reporting. The policy provides for grave human rights violations committed since 1995 to be addressed through transitional justice mechanisms to be carried out by independent institutions established under the policy.[footnote 155]

10.8.2 The ACHPR July 2025 report noted that the Ethiopian delegation stated that, following the EHRC-OHCHR joint investigation into violations committed during the northern conflict, the government established an Inter-Ministerial Task Force to implement the investigation’s recommendations. According to the delegation, the Task Force created four specialised committees and collected more than 10,000 victim and witness statements. The delegation also stated that agreement had been reached to establish an independent Special Prosecution Office and a dedicated special bench to deal with transitional justice cases involving serious human rights violations committed since 1995.[footnote 156]

10.8.3 However, the Amnesty International State of the World’s Human Rights 2025 report observed that the transitional justice process remained stalled and that there had been no justice or accountability for crimes under international law committed during the Tigray conflict.[footnote 157] HRW similarly stated in June 2026 that impunity remained widespread and that the promised transitional justice process had completely stalled.[footnote 158]

10.8.4 The GoE August 2024 report to the UPR stated that the authorities had sought to hold perpetrators of grave human rights violations accountable through existing judicial mechanisms. According to the report, prosecutors filed 42 cases involving 2,117 defendants accused of extrajudicial killings and other crimes committed in the context of conflicts during the reporting period. The defendants reportedly included senior military officials, mid-level police and military officers, and local government officials. The report also stated that the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF), through its military justice system, acted against 39 military personnel accused of serious human rights violations, including extrajudicial killings. Of these, 27 were convicted and received sentences ranging from two years’ imprisonment to life imprisonment.[footnote 159] The GoE further reported that more than 90 officials from security institutions and the prison administration had been charged in connection with torture and related offences. The report stated that a number of those charged had subsequently been found guilty and convicted.[footnote 160]

10.8.5 However, OHCHR August 2024 UPR report noted: ‘The Human Rights Committee expressed concern about the impunity enjoyed by perpetrators of torture and ill-treatment, including high-ranking officers, and the slow progress made in providing effective remedies and rehabilitation to victims.’[footnote 161]

10.8.6 The HRC August 2024 UPR report stated that HRW and Physicians for Human Rights in their joint submission ‘noted challenges in the investigation and prosecution of arbitrary killings and stated that the lack of accountability had contributed to the continued practice of arbitrary executions.’[footnote 162]

10.8.7 The 2026 Human Rights Watch world report covering events in 2025 noted: ‘The government made little visible progress towards ensuring meaningful accountability for past and ongoing atrocities, while its transitional justice process effectively stalled …The EU led two joint statements at the UN Human Rights Council in March and September highlighting the lack of progress on transitional justice and an end to violations in conflict areas.’

11. Courts

11.1 Structure

11.1.1 The BTI 2026 report observed:

‘Ethiopia’s judiciary operates at both the federal and regional levels, each with its own courts. The federal system includes the Federal Supreme Court, the federal high courts and first-instance courts, while regional states have equivalent courts. Shariah courts, which are limited to handling family law cases, exist at the three federal levels, requiring mutual consent from disputing parties. The Federal Supreme Court holds ultimate authority over federal cases, and state supreme courts oversee regional matters.’[footnote 163]

11.1.2 For further information on the court system, including the federal courts, state courts, municipal and religious courts and their functions, see archived CPIN Ethiopia: Actors of Protection 2024.

11.2 Traditional courts and Community Justice Centres (CJCs)

11.2.1 The GoE October 2025 report stated that 5 regions had recognised customary justice systems during 2024/2025.[footnote 164]

11.2.2 The Bekele 2024 article observed:

‘Customary courts are not established by law, despite their constitutional recognition. They are only recognized, not created, by law. The authority of these courts stems from tradition and local customs. These courts have evolved from traditional elder councils, which do not have legal authority, but carry moral force and still operate widely as primary decision-makers in rural areas throughout Ethiopia. To name but a few of the customary courts: the Shemagelle in Amhara, the Bayito and Abo Gereb in Tigray, and the Luba Basa in Oromia. In addition, the choice [of] whether to take a dispute to regular courts or to one of those non-official forums is entirely left to the parties.’[footnote 165]

11.2.3 The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) is an independent Netherlands-based non-profit organisation specialising in access-to-justice research and justice-sector innovation.[footnote 166] In a report published in November 2024 (HiiL November 2024 report), HiiL observed:

‘Customary courts in Oromia operate on a two-tiered system. The first instance customary courts are established at the ‘Ganda’ (local) level, while appellate customary courts are found at the ‘Aanaa’ (district) level. As of July 2023, a report from the Oromia Supreme Court indicates that there are approximately 6,252 first instance customary courts serving communities in 6,355 localities … Additionally, there are currently 355 appellate customary courts functioning at the district level in the Oromia region.

‘The formalisation of customary courts in Oromia was achieved through Proclamation No.240-2021. To facilitate the effective operationalisation of these courts, the Oromia regional state also promulgated Regulation No. 10/2021, which provides comprehensive guidelines for their establishment and functioning throughout the region …’[footnote 167]

11.2.4 A November 2025 article by Tadesse Simie Metekia, a senior researcher at the Institute for Security Studies (ISS), an independent African research institute that produces research and policy analysis on governance, security, justice and human rights issues across the continent[footnote 168], noted that traditional justice mechanisms remain a widely used form of alternative dispute resolution in Ethiopia, providing accessible, affordable and culturally accepted justice rooted in indigenous systems that predate the formal judiciary.[footnote 169]

11.2.5 The same source noted that the Ministry of Justice’s 2023 Model Law on Customary Courts aims to preserve indigenous justice mechanisms while aligning them with constitutional and international human rights standards. The model law provides for free and accessible services, restricts jurisdiction to cases where parties voluntarily consent to customary adjudication, prohibits discrimination and political interference, and requires the inclusion of at least one female judge in each customary court. However, the source also highlighted a gap between the law’s objectives and implementation. Assessments of customary courts, including in Oromia, identified continuing concerns regarding human rights violations, the exclusion of women from decision-making roles, interference by local officials in proceedings, and the adjudication of matters that should fall within the jurisdiction of the formal justice system.[footnote 170]

11.2.6 Regarding Community Justice Centres, a September 2024 report by HiiL (HiiL September 2024 report) stated:

‘The idea of Community Justice Centres (CJCs) emerged as a consensus response to increase resolution rates. The model was built on the successful experiences of the government with customary courts in the Oromia region and the widespread use of the shimagille, well-established community justice providers and preferred route to conflict resolution in both urban and rural areas. The CJC model allowed communities to resolve disputes locally while aligning with international human rights standards. Yonas Birmeta, a professor at Addis Ababa University Law School, described the CJC model as a “game-changer,” blending Ethiopia’s traditional dispute resolution practices with modern systems.’[footnote 171]

11.2.7 In April 2025, HiiL reported that Community Justice Centres (CJCs) operated in Afar, Sidama and Addis Ababa.[footnote 172]

11.2.8 The Ministry of Justice reported on 16 July 2026 on the launch of the Shishinda model customary court in the South West Ethiopia Peoples’ Region, supported by the Ministry together with UNDP and HiiL. The report, which is in Amharic (unofficially translated using online translation tools) stated that customary courts had been established in 700 kebeles in the region and that more than 1,700 case files had been heard in the budget year alone, and that the Ministry would continue working with its partners to maintain and strengthen them.[footnote 173]

11.3 Access to courts (generally)

11.3.1 An April 2024 article in The Reporter on a national judges’ summit reported:

‘Less than 2,200 judges and justices across the [Amhara] region’s 220 courts (202 of which are First Instance courts) took on 826,000 civil and criminal cases last year, according to a report from the regional Supreme Court.

‘The caseload is made even more daunting by the lack of peace and security in the region, according to AbiyeKassahun [sic], president of the Amhara Regional State Supreme Court. “As a result of the current security state of our region, courts cannot be reached when needed,” he said…

‘”Over the years, the Amhara Regional State budget is growing exponentially,” said Abiye. “But, surprisingly, allocations to the courts are growing smaller and smaller.”…

‘Judges and justices across 363 of Oromia’s courts (331 of which are First Instance) took on more than 600,000 cases last year, according to a survey conducted by the Oromia Supreme Court.’[footnote 174]

11.3.2 According to the HiiL September 2024 report, more than 7 million legal problems arise annually in Ethiopia and approximately 5 million remain unresolved each year. According to the source, customary courts in Oromia processed an average of 376,000 cases annually over the previous two years and recorded high case-resolution rates.[footnote 175] The report did not provide information on the source of this data. In its November 2024 report, HiiL noted that estimated 43% of legal disputes were resolved through customary mechanisms. According to data from the Oromia Supreme Court’s Annual Performance Report, the first-instance customary courts handled 361,685 cases and resolved 294,699 (81.5%), while appellate customary courts handled 18,429 cases and resolved 15,293 (83.0%).[footnote 176]

11.3.3 According to the GoE October 2025 report, prosecutors disposed of 69,480 criminal cases during the 2024/25 reporting period and achieved a criminal conviction rate of 97%. The same source stated that customary courts in Oromia resolved 1,133,374 cases. In South West Ethiopia Regional State, 713 elders reportedly resolved 1,230 cases through mediation, while Community Justice Centres (CJCs) in Afar and Addis Ababa handled 127 and 18 cases respectively.[footnote 177] [footnote 178] The same source reported that, in selected categories of serious criminal cases, the average period between the filing of a criminal complaint and the delivery of a court judgment was one year.[footnote 179]

11.3.4 In a January 2026 article Human Rights Research Center (HRRC), an international, volunteer-led organization dedicated to making human rights research accessible beyond academic spaces[footnote 180], discussed a range of barriers to accessing justice in Ethiopia. According to the HRRC, these include legal and procedural obstacles such as complex court processes, language barriers for non-Amharic speakers, limited access to legal representation and judicial delays; economic constraints, including the cost of legal services and reportedly underfunded legal aid; geographical challenges affecting access to courts in rural and remote areas; social and cultural factors, including discrimination and the limited availability of translation services; and political and institutional concerns, including allegations of political interference, corruption and low public confidence in the judiciary. The HRRC also noted that restrictions on civil liberties may limit individuals’ ability to seek redress and hold authorities accountable.[footnote 181]

11.4 Access to courts for women

11.4.1 The HiLL November 2024 report which examined the Oromo customary courts observed:

‘According to much of the literature on justice services, traditional justice mechanisms run the risk of not aligning with contemporary human rights standards, primarily due to their roots in local patriarchal societies where gender inequality is deeply embedded. In Ethiopia, there are growing concerns that the customary justice system falls short in safeguarding human rights, especially women’s rights. However, this critique is not universal. Some elders of customary courts defend their institutions as embodying principles of equality and respect … Similarly, throughout the data, clients of these courts have reported experiences where human rights and gender equality were purposefully respected. Occasionally, in some cases priority was given to vulnerable groups such as the elderly, pregnant women, and persons with disabilities, but without discrimination against others.

‘Furthermore, during a validation workshop on the model law, representatives of [civil society organisations] CSOs underscored the insufficient participation of female judges in customary courts. This concern was further substantiated by the annual performance report of customary courts, which included visual documentation of customary court sessions across different regions of the country. The report revealed several instances where male judges dominated the proceedings, with female judges either absent or positioned in secondary roles, seated behind their male counterparts.

‘Cultural institutions that promote gender sensitivity, such as the ‘Siinqee Institution,’ have supported the involvement of women elders in some areas, notably Arsi. However, this is far from the norm …

‘In terms of equal treatment, female respondents of the impact assessment shared mixed experiences with customary courts …’[footnote 182]

11.4.2 The same source further observed that there was ‘low level of use of customary courts among women with higher education (only 5% of women with university education or above reported resorting to customary courts compared to other potential avenues for help such as family members (40%), police (30%), or formal courts (15%) …’[footnote 183]

11.4.3 Amnesty International state of the world human rights report, Ethiopia 2025 noted: ‘Women and girls continued to face conflict-related sexual violence amid the ongoing armed conflicts. No steps were taken to secure justice and reparation for survivors of such abuses in Tigray region. Outside the conflicts, women and girls experienced gender-based violence that worsened due to the collapse of the rule of law following prolonged conflict.’[footnote 184]

11.4.4 In an October 2025 position paper intended to raise awareness of barriers to justice and encourage help-seeking among women in Ethiopia, Sudan and Somalia, the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa (SIHA), a regional civil society network that works to advance women’s rights and gender equality in countries across the Horn of Africa[footnote 185], noted that women in Ethiopia faced structural and societal barriers to obtaining justice and accountability. SIHA reported that the coexistence of customary, religious and statutory legal systems made it difficult for women to identify the applicable legal process, and that the absence of state family laws in the Somali and Afar regions limited women’s ability to seek justice within those regions. It further cited research indicating that customary dispute-resolution processes in Tigray favoured men and powerful members of society; religious courts required women to be represented by a male guardian; police did not always treat reports of gender-based violence seriously and sometimes requested bribes to process or investigate cases; and the requirement for female representation in Oromia’s social courts was not always observed in practice. SIHA further noted that Ethiopian law does not criminalise marital rape and does not fully recognise certain forms of gender-based violence, including economic and psychological violence within marriage.[footnote 186]

12. Detention

12.1 Prison capacity

12.1.1 The World Prison Brief, no date, reported that as of 2015 there were 126 prisons – 6 federal and 120 regional prisons. The source, citing the US State Department, further noted the existence of many unofficial prisons. The brief recorded no figure for the official capacity of the prison system, and on occupancy level stated: ‘No official figures have been traced but according to the U.S. State Department human rights report for 2016 severe overcrowding is common.’[footnote 187]

12.1.2 The ACHPR July 2025 report stated: ‘… [T]he figures provided by the Delegation on prison infrastructure (121 prisons nationwide, including 6 federal prisons and 115 distributed across regions) and prison population (a total of 102,428 prisoners, including 2-4% women) don’t indicate the occupancy rate, which is a very determinant indicator in this area. Additionally, the Commission cannot find any detail on the duration of pre-trial detention respect [sic] in Ethiopia.’[footnote 188]

12.2 Detention conditions

12.2.1 The Government of Ethiopia’s report to the Working Group on the Universal Period Review, dated 23 August 2024 (GoE August 2024 UPR report), stated:

‘The GoE built two prison facilities in Dire Dawa and Ziway prison centres as per international standards acceptable to conditions of detention. The construction of two new prison facilities of Aba-Samuel [in Addis Ababa] and Shewarobit [in Amhara] is also being finalized, with modern cells, administrative blocks, and academic and vocational schools.

‘A significant increase in the daily subsistence budget per prisoner has been witnessed during the period under review. This includes a raise in the daily meal budget, provision of basic sanitary materials, and healthcare expenditure for prisoners. Similar initiatives are also underway in regions.

‘Federal and regional correction centers have separate quarters/zones for women inmates and juvenile offenders who are above the age of 15 years. Similarly, a Rehabilitation Center for Children in Conflict with the Law between the ages of 9 to 15, with a capacity of holding 700 inmates, has been rebuilt in Addis Ababa and became operational in September 2022. The center has 17 blocks with rooms, workshops for vocational training, classrooms, meeting halls, a library, rooms for psycho-social support, and sports facilities.’[footnote 189]

12.2.2 The Ethiopian Human Rights Commission (EHRC), in the English executive summary of its August 2025 Annual Human Rights Report covering the period from June 2024 to June 2025 (EHRC August 2025 report), noted some improvements in detention conditions, including a reduction in inhuman treatment of detainees, an increase in the food budget allocated to prisoners, and the expansion of prison infrastructure to help address overcrowding and poor sanitary conditions.[footnote 190] However, the same source observed:

‘Many of the challenges regarding conditions of detention of prisoners and detainees have either persisted or became worse …

‘The major gaps identified during EHRC’s detention centers monitoring include the fact that detainees are not provided with food in many police stations; prisoners are not provided with sufficient, quality and nutritious food although some regions have raised the daily prisoners’ food budget; detainees are subjected to torture and ill treatment in some police stations and that there is no complaint procedure in place. Children in conflict with the law are detained with adults and there are gaps in the application of the principle of separate detention for other categories of detainees. While there have been efforts to expand prison and police station infrastructure in some regions, overcrowding, poor hygiene, and a lack of basic necessities continue to be major problems across many regions. In many prison facilities, there was a severe shortage of beds and mattresses, forcing detainees to sleep on the floor in unsanitary and uncomfortable conditions. Access to healthcare and quality education services also remains insufficient in most detention centers. Furthermore, the EHRC identified serious gaps in the provision of support to prisoners with special needs.’[footnote 191]

12.2.3 In an August 2025 article on the same EHRC report, The Reporter noted: ‘The Commission found that while the treatment of detainees in prisons in Afar, Benishangul-Gumuz, and Sidama has improved, the situation elsewhere is worrying.’[footnote 192]

12.2.4 The OMCT 2025 report observed:

‘Detention conditions in Ethiopia significantly compromise the right to freedom from torture. Facilities are critically overcrowded, with occupancy rates exceeding 120%, leading to inadequate sanitation, poor ventilation, insufficient lighting, and limited access to food, clothing and medical care. Upon arrival, detainees rarely receive mental health assessments or adequate medical attention. Medical examinations following the use of force are typically insufficient, lacking thorough documentation and judicial reporting obligations.

‘Punitive and degrading practices, such as corporal and collective punishment, denial of family contact, restrictive diets and restricted drinking water are frequently employed against detainees. Solitary confinement lacks adequate safeguards and is routinely applied, potentially affecting vulnerable groups such as pregnant women and mothers with infants. Ethnic groups, notably Tigrayan and Amhara detainees, are regularly subjected to discriminatory and intrusive body searches.’[footnote 193]

13. Human rights violations by security forces

13.1 General

13.1.1 For information on human rights violations by the security forces in the context of conflict and post-conflict insecurity, see the following CPINs: Oromos, the Oromo Liberation Front and the Oromo Liberation Army, Amhara and Amhara opposition groups, and Tigrayans and the Tigrayan People’s Liberation Front.

13.2 Torture and ill-treatment

13.2.1 The OHCHR August 2024 UPR report observed: ‘The Committee against Torture expressed concern about reports indicating that torture was routinely used to extract confessions and that confessions obtained through torture had been admitted as evidence of guilt in criminal trials. The Human Rights Committee expressed concern about reports that objections to the admissibility of forced confessions as evidence were frequently rejected during trials, particularly in terrorism trials …’[footnote 194]

13.2.2 A July 2025 Viewpoint article in Ethiopia Insight by Adam Denekew Mekonnen, a former lecturer of law at Bahir Dar University, noted:

‘On 18 June, the Ethiopian Parliament passed a law which amends the country’s Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing framework. The law introduces legal immunity for undercover agents who commit crimes deemed “beyond their control” during operations…

‘Article 33(4) of Proclamation No. 1387/2025 grants agents advance immunity for crimes committed while conducting undercover operations. But what exactly counts as “beyond control”? Without a specific legal definition, it could cover a vast array of abuses, from coerced confessions and illegal surveillance to violence against civilians.

‘Furthermore, the term “undercover agent” lacks a clear statutory limit. It could be expansively interpreted to include not only trained intelligence personnel but also plainclothes officers, unvetted informants, or even politically motivated civilians acting under unofficial orders…

‘Ethiopia’s existing Criminal Code accounts for such instances. Article 57 exonerates criminal liability in cases involving accident or force majeure. Article 58 provides protection where outcomes were neither intended nor reasonably foreseeable… By contrast, Article 33(4) offers a blanket advance waiver—sidestepping courts entirely.’[footnote 195]

13.2.3 The ACHPR July 2025 report noted that that ‘The Delegation informed that the Government of Ethiopia has drafted legislation on Fundamental Crimes Committed in violation of International Law, which includes a definition of torture in line with Article 1 of the Convention against Torture.’ The Commission recommended that Ethiopia ‘Finalize the adoption process of the draft Criminal Procedure and Evidence Code and ensure the inclusion of a definition of torture and the inadmissibility of any evidence gathered through coercion or torture.’[footnote 196]

13.2.4 The USSD 2024 report observed:

‘Although the constitution prohibited such practices, there were reports security officials tortured and otherwise abused detainees.

‘According to the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), HRW, Physicians for Human Rights, Amnesty International, and numerous media reports, the government engaged in torture in its security operations and failed to hold government actors accused of torture accountable.

‘In a May report submitted to the African Commission on Human and People’s Rights, the OMCT and the [Ethiopia Human Rights Council] EHRCO [an independent, non-profit making, non-partisan human rights organization[footnote 197]] highlighted several incidents where federal government security forces, including regional police, committed acts of torture. The report stated that government security forces subjected civilians in the Kelafo District of the Somali Region to physical torture, such as flogging and covering their heads with plastic bags filled with pepper powder, resulting in permanent physical injuries and loss of eyesight.

‘According to the EHRC, HRW, [Centre for the Advancement of Rights and Democracy] CARD [a civil society organization whose mission is to advance a conducive civic, media, and digital space for the respect of human rights and cultivation of democratic mass culture in Ethiopia[footnote 198]], and media reports, both the government and militias in Amhara, Oromia, and Tigray regions engaged in torture and mistreatment of civilians and captured combatants. Victims were reportedly beaten with electric cables and metal pipes, detained incommunicado, threatened with guns to their heads, and deprived of food and water. Civilians in western Tigray were reportedly tortured and mistreated mainly because of their ethnic identities. Elsewhere, captured soldiers and fighters, as well as civilian family members of combatants or government officials and those suspected of providing support to combatants or government officials, were reportedly tortured.

‘According to the EHRC annual report, in Oromia Region a government militia, the Oromia Regional Police, and the ENDF … widely beat, tortured, and handcuffed inmates for inhuman periods of time.’[footnote 199]

13.2.5 The Global Torture Index (GTI), an expert-informed assessment tool that measures countries’ vulnerability to torture and ill-treatment[footnote 200], reported in its 2025 Ethiopia factsheet:

‘Torture remains widespread and systemic in Ethiopia, significantly fuelled by ongoing internal conflicts and political instability. For 2025, the Global Torture Index classifies the country as facing a very high risk of torture and ill treatment, based on data collected in 2023 and 2024. Key areas of concern include police brutality, conditions within detention centres and abuses facilitated under emergency laws, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Tigray, Oromia, Afar, and Amhara. Key violations involve psychological pressure, physical violence, and forced confessions during interrogations and detention. Victims, including political opponents, journalists, human rights defenders, lawyers, judges, religious leaders and various ethnic minority groups like Tigrayans and Amhara, regularly face discriminatory treatment. Torture methods include severe beatings, confinement in cramped spaces, enforced stress positions for long periods, prolonged solitary confinement in military camps, sleep and food deprivation, lack of access to medical care, detention in harsh climatic conditions and the alarming practice of incommunicado detention, all aimed at silencing dissent or extracting confessions.’[footnote 201]

13.3 Extrajudicial killings and excessive use of force

13.3.1 The OHCHR August 2024 UPR report observed: ‘The [Human Rights Committee] … expressed its concern that excessive use of force, including lethal force, by police and security forces remained widespread, notably in the context of protests, and that the existing legal framework for the use of force and firearms by State agents was inadequate.’[footnote 202]

13.3.2 In its August 2024 UPR report HRC reported that several stakeholders alleged an increase in extrajudicial, summary and arbitrary killings in Ethiopia since the previous review. The HRC noted that a joint submission by Human Rights Watch (HRW) and Physicians for Human Rights (PHR) alleged that government security forces and non-state armed groups had carried out extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions during armed conflict and periods of unrest. The HRC also reported that the Ethiopian Human Rights Council (EHRCO) and the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) stated that violations of the rights to life and personal security had been committed by both state and non-state armed actors. In addition, a joint submission by the Oromia Support Group UK and Oromia Support Group Australia alleged that government security forces and Fano militia were responsible for large numbers of extrajudicial killings of Oromo civilians, including persons suspected of links to the Oromo Liberation Army.[footnote 203]

13.3.3 A January 2025 news report by The Reporter, a privately owned Ethiopian English-language news publication[footnote 204], reported that the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission (EHRC) had identified an increase in alleged extrajudicial killings and enforced disappearances in several regions of Ethiopia. According to the report, the EHRC’s findings were based on investigations conducted between September 2024 and January 2025, drawing on testimonies from victims, family members and local organisations. The EHRC reported cases in the Amhara and Oromia regions and other conflict-affected areas, and stated that many individuals remained unaccounted for, with families unable to obtain information about their whereabouts.[footnote 205]

13.3.4 In an August 2025 article on the EHRC’s annual report, The Reporter noted:

‘The 152-page report lists countless cases in which citizens are arbitrarily killed by government security forces, as well as armed forces like Fano in Amhara and OLF-Shene in Oromia…

‘The Commission states that civilians have repeatedly been killed during clashes between government forces and armed groups in Amhara and Oromia. Civilians are often accused of supporting the other side by both Fano and government forces, with the accusations often ending in murder, according to the report.

‘Similar scenarios have occurred in Oromia, where civilians are killed by government forces or OLF-Shene on suspicion of aiding the other side.’[footnote 206]

13.3.5 The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) is an independent, non-profit organisation that collects and analyses data on political violence, protest events and conflict-related developments worldwide. ACLED provides near real-time event data based on information gathered from a range of sources, including media reports, international organisations, NGOs and local partners. Its datasets are widely used by researchers, governments, international organisations and humanitarian actors to monitor patterns and trends of conflict and insecurity.[footnote 207]

13.4 Arbitrary arrest and detention

13.4.1 The USSD 2024 report noted that despite constitutional and legal safeguards against arbitrary arrest and detention, such protections were not consistently observed in practice. According to the USSD, there were reports of widespread arbitrary detention, including the continued detention of thousands of ethnic Amhara and Oromo individuals following the end of the state of emergency in June 2024.The report also noted that authorities sometimes failed to comply with court orders for release by filing new charges, appealing bail decisions or transferring detainees to other jurisdictions. In addition, seven Oromo Liberation Front (OLF) leaders were reportedly released in September 2024 after being detained for more than four years without charge despite multiple court orders for their release.[footnote 208]

13.4.2 The OHCHR August 2024 UPR report observed: ‘The Human Rights Committee expressed concern about reports of large-scale arbitrary detention and stated that Ethiopia should investigate all allegations of arbitrary arrest and detention and ensure that alleged perpetrators were prosecuted and, if convicted, punished with appropriate penalties and should ensure that anyone who was detained arbitrarily was released without conditions and adequately compensated.’[footnote 209]

13.4.3 In a December 2024 article, The Reporter, citing findings from EHRC investigation in Oromia, reported that children as young as 11 were forcibly and arbitrarily detained as part of mobilisation efforts for regional military forces. According to the EHRC findings reported by The Reporter, children were rounded up and detained, including in Shashemene where they were held in a convention hall under the pretext of receiving military training. The report also documented the detention of mentally ill individuals and stated that police, military personnel and local militia forces were responsible for these detentions, often targeting people during their daily activities. The EHRC further stated that, because Ethiopia’s national security forces did not accept unwilling recruits, the issue was not one of conscription but rather of arbitrary and unlawful detention.[footnote 210]

13.4.4 The BTI 2026 report (covering events from February 2023 to January 2025) stated: ‘Civil society groups and individuals alike are regularly arrested, intimidated and accused of supporting anti-government groups or agendas.’[footnote 211]

13.4.5 The EHRC 2025 report observed that arbitrary and prolonged detention remained a concern. The EHRC observed that, despite the lifting of the state of emergency in Amhara Region in June 2024, practices associated with the state of emergency continued, including mass arrests and detention in informal facilities, prisons, police stations and military camps without court appearances. Arbitrary and unlawful detention including arrests without warrants, detention without judicial oversight, and the transfer of detainees between police stations also occurred in Oromia in connection with the ongoing conflict.[footnote 212]

13.4.6 The OMCT 2025 report observed:

‘Several reports state that incommunicado detention is practiced in Ethiopia, often denying detainees access to lawyers and family members for weeks or even months. In politically motivated cases, the right to bail is often denied even after court decisions. Following the August 2023 state of emergency, thousands of individuals in the Amhara region, as well as ethnic Amhara people were reportedly detained arbitrarily. Moreover, the absence of mandatory video recording during interrogations or arrests makes the independent verification of police conduct difficult, further entrenching a culture of impunity. Complaints against law enforcement rarely result in accountability or disciplinary action, and investigations typically lack independence and effectiveness.’[footnote 213]

13.4.7 Sources reporting on media freedom in 2026 indicated the continued arrest and detention of journalists and media workers. In February 2026 HRW reported that journalists working for independent media outlets faced harassment, arbitrary arrest and periods of incommunicado detention, and documented cases of journalists and media workers being arrested, detained, abducted or otherwise restricted by the authorities in various parts of Ethiopia, including Addis Ababa and the Somali Region.[footnote 214] In May 2026, Amnesty International similarly reported a renewed crackdown on journalists, including detentions and alleged enforced disappearances, and cited the detention of Addis Standard managing editor Million Beyene, who was reportedly held for two weeks without access to his lawyer or family, with Amnesty assessing that the detention appeared to be linked to his journalistic work.[footnote 215]

13.4.8 BBC Monitoring, citing The Reporter, stated in June 2026 that the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission (EHRC) had documented the continued occurrence of arbitrary arrests without court orders in several parts of the country, despite reporting that 2,143 detainees had been released during the previous 11 months.[footnote 216] Separately, HRW reported that authorities and security forces in Western Tigray continued to arbitrarily detain ethnic Tigrayans while also imposing severe restrictions on their freedom of movement, employment and access to services.[footnote 217]

13.4.9 An August 2026 analysis by the Addis Standard reported arbitrary detentions linked to military recruitment in parts of Oromia including Sheger City near Addis Ababa. According to the report, families alleged that young people had been taken against their will, and, in some cases, money was demanded for their release. The report stated that the EHRC had opened an investigation into allegations of forced conscription and met senior ENDF officials in 2025 to discuss complaints received, although the outcome had not been made public. The Oromia regional government rejected allegations of widespread forced conscription and related abuses, describing such claims as unfounded propaganda.[footnote 218]

13.6 Enforced disappearance

13.6.1 The EHRC noted in its submission to the UN Human Rights Council’s 57th session held between 9 September and 9 October 2024 that Ethiopian law provides safeguards against enforced disappearance. The Constitution protects liberty and security of person, while the Criminal Code criminalises enforced disappearance as an international crime and, in certain circumstances during armed conflict, as a war crime. Other domestic provisions also criminalise illegal restraint and abduction.[footnote 227]

13.6.2 However, according to the same source over the previous three years, it had investigated and documented more than 200 cases that may constitute enforced disappearance. Some individuals were subsequently released or located after being held for up to eight months in irregular detention facilities or incommunicado. In its June 2024 annual report, the EHRC documented 42 people taken from Addis Ababa whose whereabouts remained unknown at the time of reporting. Witness accounts indicated that, in most cases, individuals were reportedly taken by government security authorities, including the police, national intelligence and military. The EHRC also identified a pattern of detainees disappearing from regular detention facilities following prolonged arbitrary detention, including alleged transfers to irregular facilities or military camps. In some cases, available evidence gave the EHRC reasonable grounds to believe that victims had been unlawfully killed, while the absence of arrest, detention and transfer records impeded investigation.[footnote 228]

13.6.3 The USSD 2024 country report noted that there were enforced disappearances by, or on behalf of, government authorities in Ethiopia. It cited numerous cases involving government critics, including political commentators, journalists, activists and former military officers, as well as detention in informal or undisclosed locations where authorities reportedly concealed individuals’ fate or whereabouts. In Tigray, enforced disappearances reportedly continued despite having decreased following the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement (CoHA), with individuals allegedly abducted by government agents or groups acting with government authorisation, support or acquiescence. The report also noted that thousands of Tigrayans were reportedly arbitrarily detained at unknown locations in western Tigray.[footnote 229]

14. Oversight mechanisms

14.1.1 For more information on oversight mechanisms including regulation, the EHRC, the office of the ombudsman, monitoring of detention centres and complaint systems, see the archived CPIN Ethiopia: Actors of protection, February 2024.

14.1.2 A report by the Government of Ethiopia (GoE) to the Working Group on the Universal Periodic Review (UPR), dated 23 August 2024, noted Proclamation No. 1307/2023 expanded the remit of the office of the ombudsman to include the investigation of administrative abuses committed by private entities.[footnote 233]

14.1.3 The same source reported that in 2023/2024, the EHRC ‘conducted 45 investigations and 32 systemic investigations related to government maladministration and 90% of administrative complaints have been resolved.’[footnote 234] The MoJ October 2025 report stated that between 2020 to 2025, criminal proceedings for human rights violations had been initiated against 19 police officers, resulting in 4 convictions.[footnote 235]

14.1.4 The ACHPR July 2025 report noted that: ‘The Commission notes with satisfaction that the EHRC is mandated to conduct regular and unannounced visits to all places of detention, including police stations and prisons, to assess compliance with human rights standards.’[footnote 236]

14.1.5 The MoJ October 2025 report stated that between 2020 and 2025 the MoJ monitored approximately 112,000 detainees and prisoners as part of its human rights protection activities.[footnote 237]

14.1.6 The OMCT 2025 report noted that victims of torture in Ethiopia had limited access to effective remedies, with legal aid, psychological support and meaningful access to justice remaining limited. It assessed complaint mechanisms as largely ineffective and lacking independence, with complainants and detainees reportedly facing intimidation and reprisals. The OMCT also noted the absence of a National Preventive Mechanism [an independent body established under the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture with a mandate to prevent torture and ill-treatment through regular monitoring of places of detention[footnote 238] and reported limitations on independent monitoring of detention facilities, including restrictions on access by the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission.[footnote 239]

14.1.7 In an August 2025 article on the EHRC’s annual report, The Reporter noted:

‘In a surprising departure from protocol, Commissioner Berhanu Adelo, who replaced Daniel Bekele (PhD) this year, disclosed EHRC was not called to present its annual report to Parliament this time around…

‘The Commission reports it received 1,258 appeals and complaints from individuals and groups during the year, of which 416 are from Addis Ababa. More than half of the complaints concerned breaches of political and civic rights, according to the report…

‘The report states the government has opposed the Commission’s attempts to visit detention and prison facilities in the Amhara region. Its officers managed to visit just five facilities in the region during the reporting period.’[footnote 240]
